summary: Sirach 35 links worship and daily conduct: keeping the law, returning kindness, giving alms, and turning from wickedness are described in sacrificial language. The chapter then urges generous offerings without trying to bribe God, because the Lord judges without favoritism and hears the wronged, the fatherless, the widow, and the humble. It closes with confidence that God will judge unrighteousness and make his people rejoice in mercy.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers Sirach's concern that worship, justice, generosity, and prayer belong together. It shows temple language and social ethics side by side, without treating gifts to God as a way to override injustice.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew work into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jewish readers who wanted instruction for living according to the law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, priesthood, scribal study, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean pressures forming the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic lines, using paired sayings, direct exhortation, worship language, and vivid comparisons.

outline.heading: Obedience And Mercy As Offerings
outline.note: Keeping commandments, returning kindness, giving alms, and departing from wickedness are described as offerings and sacrifice.

outline.heading: Do Not Come Empty
outline.note: The reader is told to appear before the Lord with what the commandment requires.

outline.heading: Generous Gifts Before The Most High
outline.note: The righteous offering is acceptable, and gifts are to be given with generosity, gladness, and proportion to what God has given.

outline.heading: No Bribe For The Judge
outline.note: The Lord is judge without favoritism, so gifts cannot purchase acceptance while the poor, wronged, fatherless, and widow cry out.

outline.heading: The Humble Prayer Reaches God
outline.note: The one who serves God acceptably and the humble person are pictured as praying until God visits and judges righteously.

outline.heading: Judgment And Mercy
outline.note: The Lord is portrayed as acting against the unmerciful and unrighteous, judging his people’s cause, and bringing mercy like rain in drought.

keyVerses.text: To depart from wickedness pleases the Lord. To depart from unrighteousness is an atoning sacrifice.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter’s opening claim most plainly: moral turning is not separate from worship.

keyVerses.text: Give to the Most High according as he has given. As your hand has found, give generously.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the chapter’s call to generosity as a response to what God has already given.

keyVerses.text: Don’t plan to bribe him with gifts, for he will not receive them. Don’t set your mind on an unrighteous sacrifice, For the Lord is the judge, and with him is no respect of persons.
keyVerses.why: This verse prevents the offering language from becoming a way to buy divine favor or cover injustice.

keyVerses.text: The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds. until it comes near, he will not be comforted. He won’t depart until the Most High visits and he judges righteously and executes judgment.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the chapter’s strongest image of prayer from the humble reaching God and waiting for righteous judgment.

questions.question: Why does the chapter compare obedience and kindness to sacrifices?
questions.answer: The first three verses use worship language for acts such as keeping the law, heeding commandments, returning kindness, giving alms, and departing from wickedness. The point is not that temple offerings disappear, since the chapter also speaks about appearing before the Lord and bringing gifts. It places ritual giving and righteous conduct in the same moral field.

questions.question: What does “don’t appear in the presence of the Lord empty” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, the phrase belongs to a section about gifts and commandment-keeping. Verse 5 says these things are done because of the commandment, and the next verses speak of offerings, first fruits, tithes, and generosity. The verse calls for worship that brings what is due, not a merely inward claim to devotion.

questions.question: What are “first fruits” and “tithe” in this chapter?
questions.answer: The “first fruits” are the first yield of one’s work or produce, and a “tithe” is a tenth set apart for worship. The chapter calls for concrete gifts: do not reduce the first fruits, give with a cheerful face, and dedicate the tithe with gladness. Generosity responds to what God has given.

questions.question: Does verse 11 promise that every generous gift will return as seven times more?
questions.answer: Verse 11 says, “For the Lord repays, and he will repay you sevenfold.” This assurance of generous repayment is followed immediately by a warning against trying to bribe God with gifts. The chapter gives no schedule or form for the repayment, and it does not present giving as a technique for forcing a return.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say God cannot be bribed?
questions.answer: Verse 12 directly rejects planning to bribe God with gifts and calls an unrighteous sacrifice unacceptable. The reason given is that the Lord is the judge and shows “no respect of persons.” In this chapter, generosity matters, but it cannot cancel injustice or manipulate judgment.

questions.question: Who receives special attention when the chapter speaks about prayer?
questions.answer: The chapter names the poor man, the wronged person, the fatherless, the widow, and the humble. It says God listens to the wronged and does not despise the supplication of the fatherless or the widow. These verses focus on people with little social protection whose cries are brought before God.

questions.question: What does “supplication” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: “Supplication” means an earnest plea or prayer. The word appears when the fatherless or widow pours out a tale, and again when the one who serves God is accepted. The chapter presents supplication not as polished speech but as a plea that reaches God.

questions.question: Why does the prayer of the humble “pierce the clouds”?
questions.answer: Verse 17 uses a vivid image to say that the humble person’s prayer reaches the Most High. The same verse says the person will not be comforted or depart until God visits, judges righteously, and executes judgment. The image emphasizes persistence and divine attention, not a mechanical process.

questions.question: How should readers understand the violent judgment language near the end?
questions.answer: Verses 18–19 depict severe divine judgment: the unmerciful are crushed, arrogant rulers are brought down, and the Lord takes vengeance on the nations. These acts are assigned to God, not given as instructions for students to attack others. The passage insists that oppression will be answered and closes with mercy welcomed like rain during drought.

glossary.def: A sacrifice named in verse 1. In this chapter it is used as a comparison for heeding the commandments.
Gifts given to help those in need. Verse 2 treats giving alms as worshipful action, comparing it to a thank offering.
The first yield from one’s work or produce. Verse 8 tells the reader not to reduce the first fruits of the hands.
A tenth set apart for worship. Verse 9 says to dedicate it with gladness.
Favoritism or partiality. Verse 12 says the Lord, as judge, does not show it.
An earnest plea or prayer. The chapter uses it for the cry of the vulnerable and for prayer that reaches God.
